newsitem.title: UK: UK grain prices close to trigger dormant support.
newsitem.headline: UK grain prices close to trigger dormant support.

text.p: British farmers, watching grain prices tumble, are waking up to the fact that a dormant clause in European Union (EU) intervention rules might protect them from further losses.
Most of the wheat produced in the UK is the non-breadmaking, feed type that doesn't qualify for intervention stores.

But an arcane safety mechanism in European farm regulations states that action may be taken if the price of feed wheat falls more than five percent below milling wheat or barley at a time when either of those may go into intervention.
The clause was introduced in 1992 to prevent a dramatic fall in feed wheat prices disturbing the markets for other grains.

The premium on feed wheat over barley has made the rule somewhat redundant over recent years but Steve Thornhill, head of marketing and economics at the Home-Grown Cereals Authority (HGCA), reckoned prices were edging close to the trigger.
Spot feed wheat has already shrunk to 95 stg a tonne in eastern ports. It traded three stg below barley which itself is only an inch above the intervention price of 97.40 stg.
In other words, the EU support mechanism could be activated if feed wheat prices dropped to around 92.50 stg.
"We are talking about break-even costs on wheat depending on yield levels," said Bernard Martin of consultancy firm ADAS.
The situation is also helped by the mathematics of the agrimonetary grid -- a system of green rates used to convert Ecu-based European subsidies into national currencies.

According to complex agrimonetary rules, sterling, which revalued in the grid after rallying in currency markets last week, can not revalue again before the end of this year. Hence if the UK currency continues to advance it may force grain prices down without putting extra pressure on the intervention price set by the green rate.
But grain analysts said that even if the EU mechanism was set in motion, just what level of support would the European Union (EU) Commission be prepared to consider was a wild guess.

For one thing, the EU was unlikely to start a costly intervention on feed wheat at a time when it's still grappling with a huge bill from the beef sector after the crisis over BSE (Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy) struck beef sales this year.
"The text is open to interpretation. One could think of a special refund, transport allowance or storage aid," said Bill Niven, managing director of United Grain Producers.
"Perhaps it is more likely to open an export tender for UK feed wheat," said the HGCA's Thornhill.
Another option could be to lower weekly refunds to ease the flow of exports. The situation could even correct itself if UK prices were cheap enough to generate intra-EU business.

Competitive prices have enabled UK traders to export surplus wheat and traders now estimate shipments to reach 2.8 million tonnes by the end of January out of an exportable surplus of up to five million.
But the situation may not last once other sellers, like France, start an aggressive export campaign, traders said.
The EU may also not be sympathetic to producers' demands after windfall profits on the farm earlier this year when tight supplies sent wheat prices to all-time highs.
"By the time the Commission will decide, the opportunity will have gone," said one trader.
